at.step: A cluster of ten nodes becomes eleven. Plain modulo hashing moves almost every key; a ring moves about one key in eleven; a fixed-slot table moves exactly the slots an operator chooses to move. But one key is hot, and none of those three placement schemes notices by itself. Predict: when one key carries a quarter of all traffic, does giving every node a thousand points on the ring instead of one actually help that key?
Three real answers to the same question: which machine owns this key? Cassandra's token ring, Redis Cluster's fixed slot table, Kafka's plain modulo hashing.
Cassandra names its own mechanism directly: consistent hashing using a token ring. Virtual nodes, several tokens per physical node, fix the imbalance a single token per node has on a small cluster.

Redis Cluster is not a ring at all. The key space is a fixed table of slots; a key's slot is a hash of the key, taken modulo the slot count; each master node owns a subset of the slots directly, not a subset of a numeric range.

Kafka's keyed partitioner computes a hash of the key, taken modulo the current partition count. Plain modulo hashing, with no stability property at all: change the partition count, and the mapping changes almost everywhere.
Predict, then measured: growing ten nodes to eleven. How much of the key space does each of the three schemes actually move?
Measured: the ring moves about one key in nine; the fixed-slot table moves a comparably small, operator-controlled share; modulo hashing moves almost every key.

Two different mechanics for a similar-sized move. A ring's new node claims a token range from its neighbors automatically. A slot table's operator moves whole slots one at a time, each going through an explicit migrating and importing handshake: data is never moved between nodes except when resharding.
The shared blind spot: every one of these three schemes balances keys, never load. One hot key still lands on exactly one node, whichever scheme placed it there.

Measured: the same hot key, now under a ring with a thousand points per node instead of one. Which node ends up owning it can change, but how overloaded that node becomes does not systematically improve: the key still hashes to exactly one point, however many points exist.

HAProxy's real knob for this: hash-balance-factor. A server already carrying more than its share of the average load is skipped, and the next candidate the same hash would choose is tried instead, until one with room is found. The feature is off by default.
Measured: the same hot key, now under bounded-load placement at HAProxy's own example factor. The busiest node's share drops from several times the average down to close to the factor itself.

items.item: Python's built-in hash() was caught and replaced with a fixed MD5-based digest before any number was written into OUTLINE.md or the reel, after an early run of examples.py produced a different result on a second invocation in the same session (CPython randomizes str hashing per process unless PYTHONHASHSEED is set).

Cassandra's current default num_tokens for new clusters was left explicitly unresolved rather than guessed, after reading the production configuration guide and finding only example values and guidance, not a stated current shipped default.

The claim that Redis Cluster and Kafka 'are not consistent-hashing rings' is checked directly against what each source's own mechanism actually is (a flat slot table; a one-line modulo), not merely asserted by contrast with Cassandra.
